entries.1:1: God gave a message to the prophet Zechariah at a specific, datable moment in history. It reminds us that God really does speak into real times and real lives, including ours.
entries.1:2: God was deeply angry with the earlier generation because of their sin. Their story is a warning that God takes wrongdoing seriously.
entries.1:3: God invites his people to turn back to him, and he promises to turn back to them. Coming back to God is never met with a cold shoulder.
entries.1:4: The earlier prophets urged people to stop doing evil, but that generation ignored them. We are urged not to repeat the same mistake of ignoring God's warnings.
entries.1:5: The ancestors and prophets have died and are gone. Human generations pass away, so the important question is whether we listen while we can.
entries.1:6: God's words did come true, and the people finally admitted that God had treated them as their actions deserved. God's warnings are reliable, so it is wise to take them to heart.
entries.1:7: God spoke to Zechariah again a few months later, on a specific date. God keeps speaking to his people over time, not just once.
entries.1:8: Zechariah saw a vision at night of a rider on a red horse among the trees, with other horses of various colors behind him. God sometimes communicates through vivid pictures that need explaining.
entries.1:9: Zechariah asked what the vision meant, and the angel promised to explain it. It is fine to ask God questions and to want to understand what he is showing you.
entries.1:10: The rider explained that the horses are messengers God has sent to patrol the whole earth. God is not distant; he is watching over the whole world.
entries.1:11: The patrol reported that the whole earth was quiet and at peace. The calm around them made the troubles of God's people stand out even more.
entries.1:12: The angel asked God how long he would hold back mercy from Jerusalem and Judah, which had suffered for seventy years. It is right to bring our long, painful waiting to God and ask him how long.
entries.1:13: God answered the angel with kind and comforting words. God's response to honest questions is not harsh; he speaks comfort.
entries.1:14: God told Zechariah to announce that he cares deeply about Jerusalem and Zion. God is not indifferent to the place and people he loves.
entries.1:15: God was angry with the surrounding nations who lived at ease and made his people's suffering worse. God notices when others add to the pain of those already hurting.
entries.1:16: God promised to return to Jerusalem with mercy, to rebuild his house, and to measure out the city again. God's mercy shows itself in real restoration, not just words.
entries.1:17: God promised that the towns would again overflow with good things and that he would comfort Zion. God's comfort includes real, concrete good in everyday life.
entries.1:18: Zechariah looked up and saw a vision of four horns. Horns in this kind of picture stand for powers that scatter and defeat.
entries.1:19: The angel explained that the horns represent the powers that drove Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem away. God names the forces that have hurt his people; they are not hidden from him.
entries.1:20: God then showed Zechariah four craftsmen or metalworkers. God shows that he has a response prepared to the powers that harmed his people.
entries.1:21: The craftsmen came to terrify and throw down the nations that scattered Judah. God does not leave his people's enemies unanswered; he acts to defend them.
entries.2:1: A man appears holding a measuring line, a tool used to check how big something is. The reader is meant to picture God about to size up Jerusalem and decide what it will become.
entries.2:2: The prophet asks where the man is going, and he answers that he is measuring Jerusalem to find out its width and length. It looks like the city is being checked for limits, as if its size matters.
entries.2:3: The angel who has been speaking with the prophet steps out, and another angel comes to meet him. This sets up a message that is about to be passed along.
entries.2:4: The second angel tells the first to hurry and give the young man a message: Jerusalem will have no walls because so many people and animals will live in it. The point is that the city will grow far beyond any walled limits.
entries.2:5: God himself says he will be a wall of fire around the city and its glory inside it. The reader can trust that God's own presence, not stone walls, will keep his people safe.
entries.2:6: God calls his people to flee from the land of the north, because he has scattered them to the four winds. It is a summons to come home from exile, since God is the one who spread them out and can bring them back.
entries.2:7: God urges the people of Zion who are living in Babylon to escape while they can. The reader hears a warning to leave a place of danger and not stay put.
entries.2:8: God says he has sent his messenger to the nations that plundered his people, because anyone who harms them is harming what is closest to God's heart. The reader learns that God takes attacks on his people personally.
entries.2:9: God will raise his hand against those nations, and their own servants will plunder them instead. When this happens, people will know that God really did send his messenger.
entries.2:10: God tells his people to sing for joy because he is coming to live among them. The reader is invited to celebrate that God's presence will be right there with his people.
entries.2:11: Many nations will join themselves to the Lord and become his people, and he will live among them. The reader sees that God's welcome reaches beyond one nation to people everywhere.
entries.2:12: God will claim Judah as his own special possession in the holy land, and Jerusalem will belong to him again. The reader is assured that God has not abandoned his people or his city.
entries.2:13: Everyone is told to be silent before the Lord, because he has woken up and come out from his holy dwelling place. The reader should pause in quiet awe, since God is on the move and about to act.
entries.3:1: Joshua the high priest stands before God's angel while an accuser stands ready to bring charges against him. It shows that God's people can face accusation, but they are still standing in God's presence.
entries.3:2: The Lord rebukes the accuser and defends Jerusalem, calling it a branch snatched from a fire. It means God himself takes your side against accusation and rescues people who were nearly destroyed.
entries.3:3: Joshua is standing before the angel wearing filthy clothes, which picture guilt and sin. It means sin leaves a person unfit to stand before God on their own.
entries.3:4: The command is given to strip off the filthy clothes and dress Joshua in clean ones. It means God does not just forgive; he removes the shame and gives a fresh standing.
entries.3:5: A clean turban is placed on Joshua's head and he is dressed in clean robes, and God declares his sin taken away. It means God's cleansing is complete, covering the whole person.
entries.3:6: The angel of the Lord speaks solemnly to Joshua. It means God is about to give him a serious charge and promise, not casual words.
entries.3:7: God promises that if Joshua walks in his ways and guards his charge, he will have authority in the temple and free access among God's servants. It means faithfulness to God brings real responsibility and nearness to him.
entries.3:8: Joshua and his fellow priests are a sign pointing to someone greater, God's servant called the Branch. It means the priests' story is a preview of the coming leader God will send.
entries.3:9: A single stone with seven eyes is set before Joshua, and God says he will engrave it and remove the land's sin in one day. It means God himself will accomplish full cleansing, and it will be his work, not ours.
entries.3:10: In that day people will invite one another to sit under their vines and fig trees. It means God's forgiveness leads to peace, safety, and ordinary shared joy.
entries.4:1: The angel wakes Zechariah up like someone rousing a person from sleep so he can pay attention to another vision. It reminds the reader that God sometimes has to get our full attention before we can understand what he is showing us.
entries.4:2: Zechariah sees a solid gold lampstand with a bowl on top, seven lamps, and seven channels feeding each lamp. The picture shows a steady supply of light, meaning God's presence and guidance keep burning without running dry.
entries.4:3: Two olive trees stand on either side of the lampstand, one at the right of the bowl and one at the left. Olive trees produce oil, so they picture a constant source keeping the light going.
entries.4:4: Zechariah asks the angel plainly what these things mean. It is fine to admit we don't understand and to ask God for understanding.
entries.4:5: The angel checks whether Zechariah really understands, and Zechariah honestly says he does not. Being honest about what we don't know is the first step to learning.
entries.4:6: God's message to Zerubbabel is that the work will be done not by human strength or muscle but by God's Spirit. Whatever we build for God depends on his power, not ours.
entries.4:7: The huge mountain of obstacles in front of Zerubbabel will be flattened, and the final stone of the building will be set in place with shouts of grace. No difficulty is too big for God to clear away.
entries.4:8: This line simply marks that God is continuing to speak to the prophet. It shows that God keeps giving his word step by step.
entries.4:9: Zerubbabel started the temple foundation and he will also finish it, which will prove the prophet was truly sent by God. God finishes what he begins through the people he calls.
entries.4:10: People should not despise small beginnings, because they will rejoice when they see Zerubbabel holding the measuring line for the finished work; the seven lamps are the eyes of the Lord scanning the whole earth. Small starts matter because God sees everything and completes his plans.
entries.4:11: Zechariah asks again about the two olive trees beside the lampstand. He is pressing for the meaning of what he saw, showing that careful questions are welcome.
entries.4:12: Zechariah asks a second time about the two olive branches that pour golden oil through the pipes. The oil flowing out pictures an ongoing supply of God's Spirit.
entries.4:13: The angel again asks if Zechariah understands, and Zechariah again says no. God is patient with those who keep asking until they grasp the truth.
entries.4:14: The two olive trees represent two anointed ones who stand beside the Lord of all the earth. They picture God's chosen servants who serve him directly and are sustained by him.
entries.5:1: Zechariah sees a large scroll flying through the air. It shows that God's message is not hidden but is moving out where everyone can see it.
entries.5:2: The scroll is huge, about thirty feet by fifteen feet. Its size shows that what God is about to declare is big and cannot be missed.
entries.5:3: The scroll stands for a curse that goes out over the whole land. It means God has finally stopped overlooking thieves and people who lie under oath, and they will be held to account.
entries.5:4: God says this curse will enter the homes of thieves and false swearers and destroy them completely, wood and stone. It means wrongdoing will not stay safely hidden inside a house; judgment will reach it there.
entries.5:5: The angel tells Zechariah to look up and see a basket-like container going out. He is being shown the next part of the vision.
entries.5:6: The container is a measuring basket, and the angel says it represents the evil done throughout the land. It pictures sin as something measured and stored up.
entries.5:7: A heavy lead cover is lifted, and a woman is sitting inside the basket. The woman is a picture of the sin being contained.
entries.5:8: The angel names the woman as Sin and shoves her back down, sealing the basket with the lead weight. It means sin is being shut up and kept from spreading further.
entries.5:9: Two women with stork-like wings, carried by the wind, lift the basket up between earth and sky. They are taking the sin away from where it was.
entries.5:10: Zechariah asks the angel where the basket is being taken. He wants to understand where this evil is going.
entries.5:11: The angel says it is going to Shinar, a distant land, to have a house built for it there. It means the evil is being removed far away and given a settled place of its own, out of God's people's land.
entries.6:1: Zechariah sees a vision of four chariots coming out from between two bronze mountains. This shows God's power and judgment moving out into the world, and reminds the reader that God is active over all the earth.
entries.6:2: The first chariot has red horses and the second has black horses. These colored horses represent different forces God sends out, and the reader should see that God directs them.
entries.6:3: The third chariot has white horses and the fourth has mixed-color horses. Each team is different, showing that God's work goes out in various ways to different places.
entries.6:4: Zechariah asks the angel who is speaking with him what these chariots mean. It is fine for the reader to ask God questions and seek understanding of what he is doing.
entries.6:5: The angel explains that these chariots go out to the four winds of heaven after standing before the Lord of all the earth. They are sent by God, who rules over the whole world, so nothing happens outside his authority.
entries.6:6: The black horses go north, the white horses go west, and the mixed-color horses go south. God's messengers are sent to specific places, showing that his purposes reach every direction.
entries.6:7: The red horses go east, and all of them ask to roam through the earth, and they are told to go. God gives his forces permission to move across the world, so the reader can trust that he is in charge of what happens.
entries.6:8: The angel says the horses going north have brought rest to the Lord's spirit in the north country. This means God's anger against evil there has been satisfied, and his work there is complete.
entries.6:9: The Lord gives Zechariah another message. This marks a shift from the vision to specific instructions for the people.
entries.6:10: Zechariah is told to collect gifts from the returning exiles, including Heldai, Tobijah, Jedaiah, and the family of Josiah, who have come back from Babylon. The reader sees that people returning from exile are bringing offerings to support God's work.
entries.6:11: He is to take the silver and gold, make a crown, and put it on the head of Zerubbabel. This honors Zerubbabel, the leader of the returned people, as part of God's plan.
entries.6:12: Zechariah is to tell Zerubbabel that God says a man called the Branch will come, and growth will come from him. This points to a future leader from God's line who will bring life and renewal.
entries.6:13: This Branch will build the Lord's temple, receive glory, and rule from his throne, with Joshua the priest beside him in peace. It shows a future where leadership and priesthood work together in harmony under God.
entries.6:14: The crown will be kept as a memorial for Heldai, Tobijah, Jedaiah, and Josiah's son, so their names stay remembered in the Lord's house. The reader learns that faithful giving to God's work is remembered.
entries.6:15: People from far away will come and help build the Lord's temple, and this will confirm that God truly sent Zechariah. It shows that God's work draws in people from everywhere, and it will happen if people obey him.
entries.7:1: This dates the message precisely: God spoke through Zechariah in a specific month of King Darius's reign. It reminds the reader that God's words come at real times in real history, not as vague ideas.
entries.7:2: People from Bethel sent two men to ask God for his favor. It shows that ordinary people cared enough about their standing with God to seek it through others.
entries.7:3: They asked the priests and prophets whether they still needed to mourn and fast in the fifth month as they had done for years. It's a question about whether an old religious practice should continue now that circumstances had changed.
entries.7:4: God responded to their question by giving Zechariah a message. The reader sees that God answers sincere questions about how we worship him.
entries.7:5: God asks whether their fasting for seventy years was really done for him or just for themselves. It challenges the reader to check whether their religious habits are truly aimed at God or merely self-focused.
entries.7:6: Even their feasting was done for their own pleasure rather than for God. It warns the reader that both sorrow and celebration can become self-centered instead of God-centered.
entries.7:7: God reminds them that he had already spoken these same things through earlier prophets, back when Jerusalem was prosperous. It shows that God's expectations don't change with circumstances, and the reader should not ignore what he has already said.
entries.7:8: This introduces another word from God through Zechariah. It signals that what follows is God's direct answer, not human opinion.
entries.7:9: God calls for fair and honest judgments and for kindness and compassion toward one another. The reader is being told that real obedience to God shows up in how they treat people.
entries.7:10: God forbids taking advantage of widows, orphans, foreigners, or the poor, and forbids plotting harm against a fellow person. It means the reader should protect the vulnerable and keep their heart free of scheming against others.
entries.7:11: The people refused to listen, turning away and covering their ears. It's a warning to the reader about how easy it is to shut out what God is saying.
entries.7:12: They made their hearts hard so they wouldn't hear God's law or the prophets, and God's anger followed. It warns the reader that repeatedly refusing to listen hardens the heart and brings serious consequences.
entries.7:13: Because they wouldn't listen to God, he wouldn't listen to them when they called. It shows the reader that ignoring God has a cost, and that he takes our refusal to hear him seriously.
entries.7:14: God scattered them among nations they didn't know, leaving the land empty and ruined. It reminds the reader that rejecting God's ways can destroy the good things he has given.
entries.8:1: God is speaking to the prophet Zechariah, and this line simply introduces that the message comes from God himself. For the reader, it means what follows isn't Zechariah's own opinion but a message from God.
entries.8:2: God says he is deeply angry about what has happened to Zion, his special city. This tells the reader that God cares strongly about his people and takes their suffering personally.
entries.8:3: God promises to return to Jerusalem and live there again, and the city will be known for faithfulness and holiness. For the reader, it means God's presence makes a place special and he keeps his promises to restore.
entries.8:4: God promises that elderly men and women will once again sit safely in Jerusalem's public squares, each leaning on a walking stick. It means the city will be peaceful and safe enough for people to grow old there.
entries.8:5: The streets will be filled with children playing. For the reader, this is a picture of a healthy, safe, happy community where families can thrive.
entries.8:6: God says that even if this seems impossible to the people who are left, it is not too hard for him. It means no situation is beyond God's ability to fix.
entries.8:7: God promises to rescue his people from faraway lands, east and west. For the reader, it means God can bring people home from anywhere and no distance is too far for him.
entries.8:8: God says he will bring his people back to live in Jerusalem and will be their God in faithfulness and right living. It means God wants a real, committed relationship with his people, not just a distant one.
entries.8:9: God encourages the people who are hearing these promises to be strong and get on with rebuilding the temple. For the reader, it means hearing God's promises should give you courage to keep working.
entries.8:10: Before this, life was hard: work didn't pay, travel wasn't safe, and people turned against each other. It describes what life is like when things are going badly and there's no peace.
entries.8:11: God says he will now treat the remaining people differently from how he treated them in the past. It means God's mercy can mark a new start after a hard time.
entries.8:12: God promises good things: crops will grow, vines will bear fruit, and rain will fall. For the reader, it means God's blessing brings real, practical good into everyday life.
entries.8:13: God says that just as his people were once an example of trouble among the nations, they will now become an example of blessing. It means God can turn a bad reputation into a good one, so there's no need to be afraid.
entries.8:14: God reminds them that when their ancestors made him angry, he carried out his warning and didn't hold back. It shows God is serious about what he says, both warnings and promises.
entries.8:15: God says he has now decided to do good to Jerusalem and his people, so they shouldn't be afraid. It means God's plans for his people are now plans for their good.
entries.8:16: God tells them what to do: tell each other the truth and make fair, peaceful decisions in their courts. For the reader, it means real faith shows up in honest words and fair treatment of others.
entries.8:17: God says don't plot harm against your neighbor and don't love making false promises, because he hates these things. It means God cares about how we treat the people around us.
entries.8:18: This line introduces another message from God through the prophet. It simply signals that what follows is God's word, not the prophet's own idea.
entries.8:19: God says the sad fasting days will become times of joy and celebration for Judah. For the reader, it means God can turn mourning into gladness, so love truth and peace.
entries.8:20: God promises that peoples and residents of many great cities will come again. It means God's reach will extend beyond one nation to many people.
entries.8:21: People from one town will urge another to go seek God's favor and worship him, and they'll go together. For the reader, it means encouraging others to seek God is a good and natural thing to do.
entries.8:22: Many strong nations and great peoples will come to worship God and ask for his favor in Jerusalem. It means people from everywhere will eventually recognize God and want to know him.
entries.8:23: In those days, ten men from different nations will grab hold of a Jewish man's clothing and say they want to go with him because they've heard God is with him. For the reader, it means when God is clearly with someone, others are drawn to what they have.
entries.9:1: God's message comes to the lands around Israel, including Damascus, showing that every nation belongs to him and is accountable to him. The reader should remember that God sees and rules over all peoples, not just their own.
entries.9:2: The neighboring cities of Hamath, Tyre, and Sidon are also included, and their reputation for wisdom will not protect them. Being clever or successful does not put anyone beyond God's reach.
entries.9:3: Tyre trusted in its wealth and built itself strong defenses, piling up silver and gold as if they were common dust. Money and security can make us feel safe, but they are not a real refuge.
entries.9:4: God will strip Tyre of its wealth and power, destroying the city by fire. Whatever we build our confidence on can be taken away, so our trust belongs in God.
entries.9:5: The nearby Philistine cities will watch Tyre fall and be terrified, and their own hopes will be disappointed. When others' false securities collapse, it is a warning to us about where we place our hope.
entries.9:6: Foreign peoples will settle in Ashdod, and the Philistines' pride will be broken. God humbles human arrogance, so we should not boast in ourselves.
entries.9:7: God will cleanse the Philistines from their idolatrous practices and bring some of them into his people, like a family within Judah. God's mercy reaches outsiders and can make anyone part of his family.
entries.9:8: God will guard his own house and his people so that no cruel oppressor will pass through them again, because he has seen their suffering. God notices our troubles and promises to protect us.
entries.9:9: Jerusalem is told to rejoice because her king is coming—righteous, victorious, and humble, riding on a donkey. This points to Jesus, and it tells us to welcome a king who comes in humility rather than force.
entries.9:10: This king will remove weapons of war and speak peace to the nations, and his rule will reach the whole earth. God's kingdom spreads through peace, not conquest, and it is meant for all peoples.
entries.9:11: Because of his covenant with his people, God will free those trapped in a hopeless, waterless pit. God keeps his promises and can rescue us even from the most hopeless situations.
entries.9:12: The prisoners are called to return with hope, and God promises to restore them double what they lost. We can live with hope because God repays his people for their suffering.
entries.9:13: God will use Judah and Ephraim like a bow and arrows to fight against Greece. God can equip and use ordinary people as his instruments in conflict.
entries.9:14: God will appear over his people, his arrow flashing like lightning, and he will come with the storm and the war cry. God himself fights for his people with power they cannot muster on their own.
entries.9:15: God will shield his people so they overcome their enemies completely, and their victory will be like a full altar in worship. God protects his people and turns their deliverance into reason for praise.
entries.9:16: On that day God will save his people and care for them like a shepherd, and they will shine like jewels in his crown. God treasures his people and provides for them.
entries.9:17: God's goodness and beauty will be seen in abundant grain and new wine that strengthen the young. God's blessings are good and life-giving, and they are meant to be enjoyed with gratitude.
entries.10:1: God tells his people to ask him for rain when the season comes, because he is the one who sends storms and makes crops grow. It means we should bring our everyday needs to God and trust him to provide.
entries.10:2: False idols and fortune-tellers give empty answers and false dreams that lead people astray like sheep without a shepherd. It warns us not to look for guidance from unreliable sources, because they leave us confused and unprotected.
entries.10:3: God is angry at the leaders who failed to care for his people, but he promises to look after his flock himself and make them strong. It means God holds leaders accountable and personally cares for those who have been neglected.
entries.10:4: God will raise up leaders and defenders from among his people, pictured as a cornerstone, a peg, a bow, and rulers. It means God provides the leadership and strength his people need.
entries.10:5: With God on their side, his people will fight like brave soldiers and overcome their enemies. It means we can face hard battles with courage because God is with us.
entries.10:6: God promises to strengthen and rescue his people and bring them home because of his mercy, as if he had never rejected them. It means God's mercy restores us even after failure, and he answers when we call.
entries.10:7: God's people will become brave and joyful, celebrating like people cheered by wine, and their children will share the joy. It means God's help brings real gladness that spreads to the next generation.
entries.10:8: God will gather his people with a signal and set them free, and their numbers will grow again. It means God actively brings his scattered people back and blesses them.
entries.10:9: Even far from home, God's people will remember him and raise their children faithfully, and they will return. It means distance and hardship cannot cut us off from remembering God and passing faith on.
entries.10:10: God promises to bring his people back from Egypt and Assyria to a land so full it will seem too small. It means God's rescue is generous and brings his people into abundance.
entries.10:11: God will clear obstacles like drying up deep waters and will humble the proud powers that held his people captive. It means no barrier or powerful enemy can stop God from setting his people free.
entries.10:12: God's people will draw their strength from him and take pride in who he is. It means our real strength and confidence come from God, not from ourselves.
entries.11:1: This pictures judgment coming like fire sweeping through Lebanon's famous cedars, so even the strongest and most impressive things are not safe. It warns the reader that nothing proud or powerful can stand when God acts in judgment.
entries.11:2: The trees are told to mourn because the great cedars have fallen, showing that when the mighty are brought down everyone around them grieves. It reminds the reader that no human greatness lasts forever.
entries.11:3: The shepherds and the lions cry out because their rich pastures and pride have been ruined. It means leaders and the strong will wail when what they relied on is taken away.
entries.11:4: God tells the prophet to act as a shepherd over a flock that is doomed to be slaughtered. It shows God still caring for people who are headed for disaster, even when others have abandoned them.
entries.11:5: The people who buy and sell the flock kill it without guilt and thank God for their profits, while the shepherds show no pity. It describes leaders who exploit the people they are supposed to protect and call their greed a blessing.
entries.11:6: God says he will stop protecting the people and let them fall into each other's hands and their king's power, leading to ruin. It warns that when people refuse God's care, they end up under harsh rulers and mutual harm.
entries.11:7: The prophet shepherds the doomed flock, especially the poor and afflicted, and takes two staffs named Beautiful and Bands to show how he will guide them. It pictures God's care using symbols of favor and unity.
entries.11:8: In a short time the prophet removes three shepherds because he is fed up with them and they resent him. It shows the breakdown of trust between God's messenger and the leaders who should have cared for the people.
entries.11:9: The prophet gives up on the flock, letting death, destruction, and mutual devouring take their course. It is a picture of what happens to people who reject good leadership and are left to themselves.
entries.11:10: The prophet breaks the staff called Beautiful, symbolizing that God's covenant protection over the peoples is being canceled. It means the special relationship of care is being withdrawn because it was rejected.
entries.11:11: The staff is broken that day, and the watching sheep traders recognize that this really was God's word through the prophet. It shows that God's warnings are confirmed even by those who profit from the situation.
entries.11:12: The prophet asks for his wages, and they pay him the insultingly small amount of thirty pieces of silver. It shows how little the people valued God's shepherd and his work among them.
entries.11:13: God tells him to throw the silver into the temple treasury, which he does, treating it as the price set on him by the people. It highlights the contempt shown to God's shepherd and points forward to the thirty pieces of silver in the gospel story.
entries.11:14: The prophet breaks the second staff, Bands, showing that the brotherly bond between Judah and Israel will be broken. It means division and conflict will replace the unity God had given his people.
entries.11:15: God tells the prophet to take up the tools of a worthless shepherd, acting out the kind of leader the people will get. It signals that bad leadership is itself a form of judgment.
entries.11:16: This shepherd will not care for the lost, the broken, or the sick, but will feed himself on the fat sheep and cripple the rest. It describes leaders who exploit and neglect the vulnerable instead of protecting them.
entries.11:17: A curse falls on the worthless shepherd who abandons the flock, and his arm and right eye will wither and go blind. It means the leader who fails his duty will lose his strength and his ability to see and guide, showing God holds leaders accountable.
entries.12:1: God introduces this message by reminding Israel that he made the heavens, the earth, and the human spirit. The one speaking is the Creator himself, so what follows carries his full authority.
entries.12:2: God will make Jerusalem like a cup that makes the surrounding nations stagger and panic when they attack the city. Those who come against God's people will be thrown into confusion.
entries.12:3: Jerusalem will become a heavy burden that hurts everyone who tries to lift it, and all the nations will gather against it. Opposing God's city will cost them dearly.
entries.12:4: God himself will confuse the enemy's horses and riders while he watches over Judah. He fights for his people by disabling those who attack them.
entries.12:5: The people of Judah will recognize that Jerusalem's real strength comes from the Lord of hosts, their God. Their confidence rests in God, not in their own power.
entries.12:6: God will make Judah like a fire that burns up the surrounding peoples, and Jerusalem will be restored to its place. God's people will be strong and their city will live again.
entries.12:7: God will rescue the ordinary people of Judah first, so that the royal family and Jerusalem's leaders don't get all the credit. God cares for the humble and keeps anyone from boasting.
entries.12:8: God will protect Jerusalem's people, and even the weakest among them will become as strong as David. God's presence makes his people far stronger than they are on their own.
entries.12:9: On that day God will set out to destroy all the nations that attack Jerusalem. God will personally deal with those who oppose his people.
entries.12:10: God will pour out a spirit of grace and prayer, and the people will look at the one they pierced and mourn deeply for him. This points to sorrow over sin and to Jesus, who was pierced for us.
entries.12:11: There will be loud, bitter mourning in Jerusalem, like the famous mourning at Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo. The grief will be real and intense, not shallow.
entries.12:12: Every family in the land will mourn, each one separately, including David's family and their wives. The sorrow is personal, and each household faces it on its own.
entries.12:13: The family of Levi and the family of Shimei will also mourn separately with their wives. Religious and ordinary families alike will share in the same deep grief.
entries.12:14: All the remaining families will mourn too, each one separately with their wives. No one is left out; the whole community grieves before God.
entries.13:1: God promises a fountain that washes away sin and uncleanness for David's family and Jerusalem's people. For the reader, it means God himself provides the cleansing we cannot give ourselves.
entries.13:2: God will remove idol worship from the land so completely that even the names of the idols are forgotten, and he will clear out false prophets and the unclean spirit. For the reader, it means God does not tolerate rival gods or lies spoken in his name.
entries.13:3: Even a false prophet's own parents will reject him and put him to death for speaking lies in the Lord's name. For the reader, it shows how seriously God takes people who claim to speak for him when they don't.
entries.13:4: False prophets will be ashamed of their visions and will stop wearing the rough hair robe that marked them as prophets, because it was used to deceive. For the reader, it means pretending to be a prophet will bring shame, not honor.
entries.13:5: The former prophet will deny being a prophet and claim he has simply been a farmer since he was young. For the reader, it shows that when false prophecy is exposed, people will scramble to distance themselves from it.
entries.13:6: When asked about wounds on his body, he will claim they came from friends rather than admit they were self-inflicted marks from idolatrous or prophetic practices. For the reader, it warns that covering up the truth with excuses does not fool God.
entries.13:7: God commands a sword to strike the shepherd who is close to him, and when the shepherd is struck the sheep scatter. For the reader, this points to the striking of God's own shepherd and the scattering that follows, while God still watches over the little ones.
entries.13:8: In the whole land, two-thirds will be cut off and perish, but one-third will survive. For the reader, it is a sober warning that judgment is real, yet God preserves a remnant.
entries.13:9: God will put that surviving third through fire, refining them like silver and testing them like gold, and they will call on him and be answered as his people. For the reader, it means hard trials can purify faith, and God remains faithful to those who call on him.
entries.14:1: God is warning that a day is coming when enemies will openly plunder Jerusalem's belongings while the people watch. It reminds the reader that judgment can come suddenly and publicly, so we should not assume we are safe from loss.
entries.14:2: God allows the nations to gather against Jerusalem, and the city suffers badly—homes looted, people harmed, half the population taken away. Yet God does not let the city be completely destroyed, showing that even in severe trouble he preserves a remnant.
entries.14:3: After the city's suffering, God himself steps in to fight against those nations like a warrior in battle. The reader can trust that God does not abandon his people but acts on their behalf at the right time.
entries.14:4: God's presence comes to the Mount of Olives, and the mountain splits in two, creating a huge valley. This shows that when God arrives, even the landscape changes—nothing can stand in the way of his purpose.
entries.14:5: The people will flee through the new valley, remembering how they fled from an earthquake long ago, and God will come with all his holy ones. It means God's arrival brings both rescue and awe, and his people are called to respond.
entries.14:6: On that day the normal cycles of heat, cold, and ice will stop. It signals that God is bringing a completely new order to the world, not just a small adjustment.
entries.14:7: There will be one endless day with no real night, and even the dark will be light. For the reader, it means God's presence removes darkness and uncertainty forever.
entries.14:8: Life-giving water will flow out of Jerusalem in both directions, all year round. This pictures God's blessing and refreshment spreading to the whole world without stopping.
entries.14:9: God will rule over the entire earth, and everyone will acknowledge him alone as Lord. The reader is reminded that history is heading toward God's universal reign, not endless chaos.
entries.14:10: The whole land will be flattened like a plain, and Jerusalem will be raised up and safely inhabited from one end to the other. It means God will make his city secure and restore normal, peaceful life.
entries.14:11: No curse will remain, and the people will live in Jerusalem without fear. This promises that God's final state for his people is safety and freedom from the effects of sin.
entries.14:12: God will strike the attacking nations with a terrible wasting disease that destroys their bodies while they stand. It shows that God's judgment on those who fight against him is severe and inescapable.
entries.14:13: God will throw the enemy nations into panic, so they turn on each other in confusion. It means God can defeat his enemies without his people having to fight, simply by causing their own plans to collapse.
entries.14:14: Judah will join the fight, and the wealth of the surrounding nations will be gathered up. The reader sees that what the enemies took by force will end up in God's people's hands.
entries.14:15: The same disease will strike the animals—horses, camels, donkeys, and livestock—along with the enemy camps. It shows that God's judgment reaches everything connected to those who oppose him.
entries.14:16: Those from the enemy nations who survive will come every year to worship the Lord and celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles. It means God's victory turns former enemies into worshipers.
entries.14:17: Any family that refuses to come worship the King will get no rain. This teaches that honoring God is not optional, and refusing him has real consequences.
entries.14:18: If Egypt refuses to come, it will receive the same plague sent on the other nations. It shows God treats everyone the same—no nation is exempt from his requirement to worship him.
entries.14:19: This is the punishment for Egypt and for any nation that skips the Feast of Tabernacles. The reader learns that worship of God is expected of all peoples, not just Israel.
entries.14:20: Even the bells on horses and the cooking pots in God's house will be set apart as holy to the Lord. It means that in God's kingdom, ordinary things are no longer common—everything is dedicated to him.
entries.14:21: Every pot in Jerusalem and Judah will be holy, used for offerings, and no traders will be left in the Lord's house. It means God's presence will make all of life sacred and will cleanse his worship of corruption.
